title: Verhagen v. Canada (Attorney General)

Parties as styled: applicant = CHRIS VERHAGEN; respondent = ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): Verhagen, applies for judicial review of a decision of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations and Employment Board (Verhagen v.
How the layers nest here: The panel is the author (layer 1). The appellant and respondent make submissions to the panel (layer 2). The lower court's or tribunal's reasons are layer 3, and what a party said there, as reported in those reasons, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The applicant, Mr. Verhagen, applies for judicial review of a decision of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations and Employment Board (Verhagen v. Canada Revenue Agency, 2025 FPSLREB 100) (the Decision). The Board rejected his application for an extension of time to remedy the untimely transmittal of his grievance.

In December 2021, Mr. Verhagen filed a grievance against his employer, the Canada Revenue Agency, alleging that its COVID-19 vaccination policy involved disciplinary action, constituted constructive dismissal, and violated his rights under section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Part I of the Constitution Act, 1982, being Schedule B to the Canada Act 1982 (U.K.), 1982, c. 11.

When his employer denied the grievance at the first level, Mr. Verhagen referred it directly to the Board for adjudication. He submitted that the applicable collective agreement allowed a direct referral because his grievance alleged he had been constructively dismissed under the policy.

His employer objected to this referral. It argued that the collective agreement required Mr. Verhagen to present the grievance at each level of the grievance process and, because he had not done so, that the Board was without jurisdiction to adjudicate it.

On March 6, 2024, the Board allowed the employer’s objection, concluded that the grievance was not properly before it and denied the referral to adjudication (the First Decision). It held that the collective agreement and the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act, S.C. 2003, c. 22, s. 2, required grievances to follow the required levels of the grievance procedure and that parties could skip levels only on mutual consent. Relying on Fauteux v. Deputy Head (Canadian Food Inspection Agency), 2022 FPSLREB 84 at paras. 48–49, it decided that the collective agreement did not entitle grievors, based solely on their own characterization of their grievance as involving a constructive dismissal, to treat their employer’s first-level reply as a final-level decision and directly refer their grievance to the Board for adjudication.

On April 8, 2024, having decided not to judicially review the First Decision, Mr. Verhagen requested his grievance be transmitted to the third level. His employer denied the grievance as untimely, because over two years had passed since the first-level grievance reply, well beyond the 10-day timeframe prescribed by the collective agreement. It similarly denied the grievance at the final level. Mr. Verhagen referred the grievance to the Board for adjudication.
The employer objected to this referral to adjudication based on, among other grounds, Mr. Verhagen’s untimely transmittal of the grievance to the third level.

Mr. Verhagen argued that the grievance had been transmitted in a timely manner. In the alternative, he asked the Board to extend the time to present his grievance “in the interest of fairness” (Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Regulations, SOR/2005-79, para. 61(b)).

In deciding whether to extend time, the Board considered several factors (Schenkman v. Treasury Board (Public Works and Government Services Canada), 2004 PSSRB 1) but placed considerable weight on whether there were clear, cogent and compelling reasons for the delay.

The Board held that the time limits to file a grievance and refer it to adjudication are brief and precise to ensure the timely, simple and expeditious resolution of disputes. It noted that they had been bargained for by the parties and the employer should rightly be entitled to rely on them. It held that they should be set aside only in extraordinary circumstances, established by clear, cogent and compelling reasons that demonstrate that extending time is in the interest of fairness.

The Board found that by insisting on directly transmitting his grievance to adjudication after the first-level denial, Mr. Verhagen had pursued a novel but ultimately unsuccessful legal strategy and that this did not constitute a cogent reason for the delay.

Even considering only the time taken by Mr. Verhagen to transmit his grievance to the third level after receiving the First Decision, the Board held that he had not provided a cogent explanation for taking 23 business days to do so—over the 10-business-day time limit for presenting a grievance at each succeeding level. It rejected his claim that the 10-business-day period did not begin to run until the deadline to judicially review the First Decision had expired.

The parties agree that the Court must review the Decision on the reasonableness standard. Mr. Verhagen must identify shortcomings or flaws in the Decision that are sufficiently central or significant to render it unreasonable (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] 4 S.C.R. 653 at para. 100 [Vavilov]).

In our view, Mr. Verhagen has not met this burden. The Decision bears all the hallmarks of reasonableness: in rational and logical reasoning that considers the arguments of the parties, the Board justifies the Decision in relation to the legal and factual constraints that bear on it.

Mr. Verhagen reiterates that, in the First Decision, the Board erred in finding that he had not followed the grievance procedure. As he did before the Board, he claims that because his grievance alleged constructive dismissal, he could refer it directly to adjudication under the collective agreement. However, because Mr. Verhagen did not judicially review the First Decision or formally request its reconsideration, it was not unreasonable for the Board to decide that the First Decision conclusively determined he had not followed the grievance procedure and, as a result, that he needed an extension of time to transmit the grievance to the third level.

Whether to grant an extension of time in the interest of fairness is a highly discretionary and factually suffused decision. Mr. Verhagen has not shown that in exercising its discretion, the Board fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it (Vavilov at para. 126). Nor was it unreasonable for the Board to depart from previous authorities, so long as it justified this departure (Vavilov at para. 131). It was entitled to find that the cases on which Mr. Verhagen relied did not afford proper weight to the importance of upholding deadlines to which the collective agreement parties had agreed.

Mr. Verhagen reiterated at the hearing before the Court that he is certain that he was constructively dismissed and that his grievance should be heard on the merits. However, unless the Board’s decision is shown to be unreasonable, we cannot intervene.
We thank Mr. Verhagen for the skill, organizational ability and eloquence he displayed in making his submissions.
The respondent agrees that there should be no costs.

Therefore, we will dismiss the application without costs. "David Stratas" J.A. "Gerald Heckman" J.A. "Elizabeth Walker" J.A.
